title: Does an Executable Generate–Validate–Repair Loop Reduce Semantic Failures in LLM-Generated NetOps Changes?
abstract: We report a fully preregistered paired experiment (CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1) that tested whether inserting an executable emulator validator into a generate→validate→repair pipeline (guarded) reduces semantic/network-level failures versus an LLM-only suggestion workflow (baseline). Using a deterministic paired design with N=120 intent→configuration tasks (40 per topology class: edge, core, leaf–spine) we produced a single shared initial candidate per task via gpt-5-mini (model_calls_used = 120) and evaluated the same candidate under both conditions. A deterministic emulator validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) enforced structured workflow policies and could trigger ≤1 repair iteration per guarded episode. Observed outcomes: baseline success = 120/120; guarded success = 120/120; contingency: n_11=120, n_10=0, n_01=0, n_00=0. Exact two-sided McNemar p = 1.0; paired-difference estimate = 0.00; bootstrap-percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Validator traces show repair_applied = false for all guarded episodes. We (1) provide a compact formal definition of the binary pass/fail scoring rule used for the confirmatory test and a concrete pass example from archived artifacts, (2) condense provenance into a single artifact-reference paragraph and move long inventories out of the main exposition, and (3) add a nearest-work comparison matrix that explicitly contrasts the present shared-generation paired design and execution accounting with the closest prior studies. We close with methodological lessons for follow-ups when generators rarely produce invalid candidates.

sections.introduction: Generative large language models (LLMs) can translate operator intent to concrete configuration commands, but syntactically plausible outputs may nonetheless violate workflow invariants (e.g., unsafe MTU/uptime sequencing or make-before-break requirements), producing semantic failures only visible in closed-loop execution. Prior work therefore proposes verification, emulation, or bounded- autonomy guardrails to detect or prevent such failures prior to enactment. Measuring the marginal effect of such validators requires careful experimental design because generator variability can mask validator impact. To isolate validator/repair effects we preregistered and executed a shared-generation paired experiment asking: Does integrating an executable emulator validator in a generate→validate→repair pipeline reduce semantic/network-level failures when enacting LLM-generated configuration changes compared to an LLM-only suggestion workflow? Our principal contribution is a preregistered, artifact-rich paired experiment (N=120) that holds the generator fixed and measures the incremental effect of an executable validator plus a bounded repair policy, together with concrete methodological recommendations for future confirmatory designs.
sections.related_work: Executable closed-loop benchmarks and verification systems demonstrate that text-level correctness does not guarantee safe enactment: emulation exposes stateful and sequencing errors (e.g., make-before-break, group- availability violations) that token-level checks miss. Representative, verified prior efforts include NetConfArena (executable closed-loop benchmarking), benchmark studies of LLM-driven configuration repair, and engineering proposals for tool-augmented, bounded-autonomy NetOps agents. These works collectively (a) motivate integrating verification/digital-twin steps into agentic NetOps and (b) typically evaluate generator and verifier jointly, so generator variance often confounds measured verifier benefits. Our shared-generation paired design isolates the verifier/repair marginal effect by scoring identical generator outputs under both conditions; this complements prior generator-focused evaluations by answering a different mechanistic question—how often the verifier/repair subsystem changes the classification of a fixed candidate.
sections.methodology:
Overview and preregistration. The study followed the preregistration CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1. Design: paired-binary with N=120 distinct intent→configuration tasks, deterministically assigned 40/40/40 across edge/core/leaf–spine topology classes. The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline; prespecified test: exact two-sided McNemar. Bootstrap-percentile 95% CI used 10,000 resamples (seed = 1729). Execution contract limited repairs to ≤1 per guarded episode and required deterministic emulator resets between tasks; exclusions for technical/instrumentation failures were defined and would be logged if observed.

Task generation, generator, and shared-candidate protocol. Tasks were produced deterministically by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; each task manifest encodes initial_state, expected_final_state, natural-language intent, required_sequence (canonical ordered operations), and difficulty metadata. For each task we executed a single shared initial generation using the declared model gpt-5-mini (execution manifest: model_calls_used = 120; stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 120}). The paired shared-candidate approach removes generator variance across paired episodes and therefore isolates the marginal influence of the validator/repair pipeline on identical candidates; the trade-off is that repair will be unused if the generator produces valid candidates for the chosen corpus.

Validator and repair semantics. The guarded pipeline invoked deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (version 5.0), an executable emulator/validator that applies task-encoded workflow policies (for example: must_be_down_for_fields, final_group_constraints, make-before-break). Validator outputs include structured fields: validation_before, validation_after, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation_count, validator_id, validator_version, and repair_applied. The preregistered repair policy attempted ≤1 repair only when validator.violation_count>0; repair prompts and traces were to be archived if produced. In this run validator.violation_count = 0 for all guarded episodes and repair_applied = false throughout.

Compact provenance and archived artifacts (condensed). To support reproducibility without inline provenance verbosity, primary execution and analysis artifacts required to reproduce reported accounting are archived and checksummed; key representative artifacts are: execution/raw_results.jsonl, execution/task_manifest.jsonl, execution/model_configuration.json, analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv, analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json, and analysis/analysis_log.jsonl. The execution and analysis manifests include detailed file-level hashes and indices; long provenance inventories and full manifests have been relocated to the archived bundle referenced by these summary artifact names (see Disclosure). No technical/instrumentation exclusions or contamination flags occurred in this run (analysis/missingness_summary.csv reports complete_pairs = 120; analysis/contamination_summary.csv is empty).

Formal binary scoring rule used in confirmatory analysis. We map archived scorer/validator fields to the binary pass/fail label used in the McNemar test with an explicit, deterministic rule (applied to each episode's scoring JSON):
- PASS if and only if all of the following hold in the episode's scoring artifact: scoring_status == "COMPLETED" AND score == 1 AND score_reason_code == "VALID_CONFIGURATION" AND validator_trace.validation_after.valid == true AND validator_trace.validation_after.violation_count == 0.
- FAIL otherwise (including parse errors, scoring_status != "COMPLETED", score != 1, or validator_trace indicates violations).
This exact rule was algorithmically applied to produce the paired binary labels archived in analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv.

Concrete pass example (archived artifact). execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json contains: scoring_status = "COMPLETED", score = 1, score_reason_code = "VALID_CONFIGURATION", validator_trace.validation_after.valid = true, validator_trace.validation_after.violation_count = 0, and normalized_response == normalized_reference_answer. Under the formal rule above this episode is labeled PASS. Concrete fail examples do not exist in the archived scoring artifacts for this run (no episode met the FAIL condition), so the confirmatory contingency table contains zero failing or discordant pairs.
sections.results:
Execution summary and confirmatory statistics. The run finished per preregistered stopping rules: planned_episode_count = 240; completed_episode_count = 240; failed_episode_count = 0; model_calls_used = 120 (one shared generation per pair). Condition-level summaries record baseline successes = 120, baseline failures = 0; guarded successes = 120, guarded failures = 0 (success rates = 1.0). The paired contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) records n_11 = 120, n_10 = 0, n_01 = 0, n_00 = 0. Exact two-sided McNemar p-value = 1.0; paired-difference estimate = 0.00. Bootstrap-percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.00, 0.00]. Validator traces report repair_applied = false for every guarded episode; consequently secondary endpoints describing repair incidence are vacuous in this run.

Per-topology counts (explicit). The preregistered deterministic partition produced 40 tasks per topology class with the following paired outcomes drawn directly from scoring artifacts:
- Edge: 40 pairs, baseline 40/40, guarded 40/40 (success rate 1.00)
- Core: 40 pairs, baseline 40/40, guarded 40/40 (success rate 1.00)

These counts appear in analysis/condition_summary.csv and in representative scoring JSONs (examples: execution/scoring/task-000001-*.json).

Representative validator diagnostics. Representative scoring artifacts show normalized_response == normalized_reference_answer; parsed_command_count equals required_command_count from the task payload; validator_trace.validation_after.valid = true; validator_trace.repair_applied = false; validator_id = deterministic_netops_validator_v5; validator_version = 5.0. The validator enforced canonical workflow constraints encoded in required_sequence fields (e.g., shut→configure→restore; make-before-break) and archived traces indicate these constraints were satisfied by generator outputs under the frozen prompt strategy.

Contamination, missingness, and reconciliation. analysis/contamination_summary.csv is empty; analysis/missingness_summary.csv reports complete_pairs = 120 with zero exclusions. The deterministic_reconciliation artifact confirms all provider-audit counts and pair accounting (n_11 = 120; hosted_model_call_event_count = 120; cross-condition cache reuse = false). These reconciliations validate internal accounting and ensure the numeric results above exactly match archived artifacts.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation and experimental lessons. The shared-generation paired design isolates the marginal effect of validator/repair by evaluating identical generator outputs under both conditions. In the present task bank and with the frozen prompting strategy, the generator produced valid candidates for every task; consequently the validator was never exercised (repair_applied = false across all guarded episodes) and could not reduce semantic failures relative to the baseline—hence the degenerate contingency (n_11 = 120) and the observed McNemar p = 1.0 and degenerate bootstrap CI. This ceiling outcome is an empirically valid but uninformative confirmatory result relative to the originally targeted paired-effect size (preregistered power calculation assumed baseline failure ≈0.40).

Design trade-offs and concrete recommendations. To measure repair utility in future confirmatory studies we recommend preregistered design adjustments grounded in archived task payload metadata (difficulty fields): (1) allow independent generation per condition or per-block pairing so the validator can intercept generator variance; (2) prespecify controlled prompt perturbations for a subset of tasks to increase generator error incidence (the current preregistration included exploratory perturbation plans and artifacts permit targeted selection); (3) stratify confirmatory power on 'very_hard' tasks or tasks with high dependency_rule_count to increase the chance of generator-induced violations; and (4) include exploratory arms with expanded repair budgets (multiple repair iterations) to measure repair convergence and cost. These recommendations are supported by the run's recorded absence of repairs and the task-manifest difficulty metadata archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl.

Threats to validity. Internal validity is strong given deterministic provisioning, exhaustive provider-call audit logs, zero exclusions, and reproducible validator traces. Construct validity is limited: validator policy encodings derive from synthetic task payloads and do not capture all vendor-specific behaviors or partial-observability telemetry. External validity is constrained by the synthetic deterministic task corpus, a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini), and a frozen prompting strategy. Conclusion validity: the preregistered power assumptions were violated by observed baseline = 0.00, rendering the confirmatory test uninformative for the preregistered effect size; the result remains a valid empirical observation that informs future design choices.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired experiment (N=120) comparing an executable generate→validate→repair pipeline against an LLM-only workflow under a deterministic harness with a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini). All 120 shared initial candidates passed the deterministic emulator validator, yielding n_11 = 120 and an observed paired-difference of 0.00 (exact McNemar p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.00], 10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). The run documents a ceiling for this curated synthetic task bank and demonstrates that a shared-generation paired design can mask repair benefits when generators rarely err. Our principal contribution is methodological: we show how a preregistered, artifact-rich paired design cleanly isolates validator/repair effects and how deterministic archival artifacts (task manifests, validator traces, provider-call audits, and reconciliation files) enable reproducible failure analysis and transparent auditing even when the primary confirmatory test is degenerate. The archived artifacts permit follow-up studies that relax the shared-generation constraint, compare generator families, expand repair budgets, and evaluate more production-rooted corpora to quantify practical repair utility under realistic generator variance.

limitations: Confirmatory scope: results are narrowly scoped to the preregistered synthetic task set, a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini), and a frozen prompting strategy; generalization to production heterogeneity is limited.
Synthetic task provenance: tasks were synthetic/deterministic and may underrepresent noisy, adversarial, or multi-vendor production incidents; external validity to live networks is constrained.

Shared-generation design: using a single shared initial generation per paired task isolates validator/repair efficacy but precludes detection of generation-variance effects; this choice contributed to the ceiling outcome and limits inference about repair utility on independently generated invalid outputs.

Validator fidelity: the deterministic emulator/validator is reproducible but simplifies heterogeneity present in multi-vendor, partially observable production environments; some real-world failure modes may not be exposed.

Statistical ceiling: baseline success reached 100% on the tested task bank, violating the preregistered power assumptions (targeted absolute reduction = 0.15) and rendering the McNemar confirmatory test uninformative for demonstrating the preregistered effect size.
